awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Efficient Wireless Power Transfer Technology Enabling Transportation Electrification
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of wireless power transfer (WPT) technology. Compared to the existing power systems, the proposed technology may increase power transfer efficiency while reducing cost and weight.  This may benefit a wide variety of applications including the charging of low-power consumer electronic devices and high-power electric vehicles (EVs).  The proposed technology is thin enough to be integrated into an electronic device without increasing its size and thickness. In addition, in EV charging applications, it may significantly improve the mobility of EVs by removing the charging cables and providing convenience to customers.  Each wireless charging pad works as an independent power system with a secured data-link service for customers to support intelligent charging demand and management.  The applications may be expanded to biomedical implants to eliminate wire-connected chargers for patients and bring benefits in healthcare area.  The proposed technology also may be applied in high-voltage power systems to support the penetration of renewable energy and distributed energy resources with high-voltage isolation capabilities.

This I-Corps project is based on the development of wireless power transfer (WPT) technology based on magnetic resonance. The proposed technology uses a resonant circuit topology design and a special magnetic coupler structure implementation.  It has been demonstrated to achieve multi-kW power transfer with over 97% efficiency across a distance up to 8 inches, which represents state-of-the-art performance. In addition, the magnetic coupler structure is optimized to confine the magnetic fields within a limited area and reduce magnetic field emissions to the surrounding environment. The technology is designed to satisfy the safety requirements proposed in both the IEEE C95.2 standard and the international commission on non-ionizing radiation protection (ICNIRP) guideline.  The proposed WPT technology targets high power, high efficiency, long distance, and compact (high power density) applications, spanning from low power to high-power systems and may be used in the power, energy, and biomedical areas.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Wireless power transfer (WPT) enables electrical energy to be delivered across an air gap without a physical plug. For transportation applications, this approach could make charging more convenient and automated. This NSF I-Corps project evaluated the commercial potential of a high-power WPT technology for transportation electrification through structured customer discovery and evidence-based commercialization planning.

During the award, the project team completed NSF I-Corps training and conducted 100 customer-discovery interviews with stakeholders from the transportation, charging-infrastructure, power-electronics, academic, and related communities. Information gathered through these activities was used to test assumptions about potential applications, customer needs, technical requirements, barriers to adoption, and commercialization pathways.

A key finding was that transportation electrification is not a single market with one uniform set of needs. Different applications and stakeholder groups have different operating conditions, purchasing processes, performance expectations, and cost constraints. Consequently, wireless charging must be evaluated for specific use cases rather than promoted through one broad value proposition.

The interviews also showed that prospective users evaluate wireless charging as a complete system solution, not only according to power-transfer efficiency. Important considerations include charging power and charging time, total cost, safety, reliability, interoperability, installation, maintenance, manufacturability, and integration with vehicles and existing infrastructure. These findings helped the team distinguish between features that are primarily of academic interest and capabilities that are essential for real-world adoption. The technology must solve a clearly defined operational or economic problem and offer meaningful benefits compared with existing charging options.

From a research perspective, the project connected power-electronics development with system-level and application-driven requirements. It established a framework for using customer evidence to guide future technical research and validation. Beyond research, the project strengthened the entrepreneurial, communication, and technology-translation skills of the PI and project team, expanded relationships with academic and industry stakeholders, and improved the team’s capacity to mentor students in customer discovery and commercialization planning.

The award focused on customer discovery rather than commercial deployment. Its principal outcome was a more rigorous, evidence-based foundation for determining how the WPT technology should proceed toward practical use. The results will support future industry collaboration, licensing, startup evaluation, and follow-on translational research. In the longer term, successful high-power wireless charging could contribute to more convenient, automated, and accessible electric-vehicle charging and support broader transportation-electrification goals.
